LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- A crowd of about 10,000 came to Dodger Stadium on Saturday, but they weren't there for a baseball game. Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shakes hands with recruiter Raul Mendez from L.A. County Probation Department. While the Dodgers were in Arizona for spring training, more than 80 employers set up employment booths in the parking lot just beyond the center field fence. To those who turned out, finding a job would be a home run. Participating companies included Coca-Cola, Lowe's and Union Bank. And government agencies including the FBI, the Social Security Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers  were there, too. All had one thing in common: They were hiring. And that was music to the ears of 30-year-old Eric Clardy. It has been a rough couple of years for Clardy. He was laid off from his job as a loan processor when the real estate market started to tank. Then, after finding work as a project manager for a plumbing company, layoffs struck again. "It's kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want," he said. Clardy said his goal is to make contact with at least 10 potential employers a day via phone, letters and the Internet. Being unemployed is hard work, too.  Watch how Clardy goes about trying to find a job » . "It was a scramble," Clardy said. "I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs." The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday's event, which they said drew about 10,000 people. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair to fill some 500 part-time jobs at the stadium during baseball season drew about 7,000 applicants. California's unemployment rate is 10.1 percent, a full 2 percentage points higher than the national rate. The state's Employment Development office estimates that nearly a half-million state residents have lost their jobs in the past year. "We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago," said Gloria Bratton Moore, who runs the state-funded Work Source job center in Los Angeles. Nonetheless, she said, "There are jobs available." But at Dodger Stadium, it was clear that competition for those available jobs is stiff. Applicants were often stacked four and five people deep in front of employer tables, and there was little chance for most of the 10,000 job seekers to make much of an impression. But organizers worked hard to pump up any flagging spirits. "Yes we can. Yes we can," Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia chanted over a loudspeaker. State lawmaker Kevin deLeon told the crowd that they are among the nation's hardest-hit in this economic downturn, but he exhorted them to not give up. "We will get out of this economic funk," he said. "We will recover soon. We've got to have hope." Garcia and deLeon's comments echoed the campaign slogans of President Obama, who recently won approval of a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package. Recruiters from the government agencies present at the job fair said that money will start creating jobs within the next few months. The Army Corps of Engineers told applicants that it is hiring for a wide variety of positions, including those for engineers, heavy-equipment operators and environmental field workers. The Commerce Department is adding more than 1 million jobs in preparation of the 2010 census, and other federal agencies are hiring as well. All of that was good news to Clardy, who left resumes and filled out applications at a number of the 80 booths cluttering the stadium's parking lot. But he remained realistic about this day's activities leading directly to a job. "It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview," he said. "Now it doesn't seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore."

outputs.L1:
LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- About 10,000 people came to Dodger Stadium on Saturday, but they were not there for a baseball game.

Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shook hands with recruiter Raul Mendez of the L.A. County Probation Department. While the Dodgers were in Arizona for spring training, more than 80 employers set up recruitment booths in the parking lot just beyond the center-field fence. For those who turned out, finding a job would have been a home run.

Participating companies included Coca-Cola, Lowe’s and Union Bank. Government agencies, including the FBI, the Social Security Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers, were also in attendance. They all had one thing in common: They were hiring.

That was welcome news for 30-year-old Eric Clardy. The past couple of years have been difficult for him. He was laid off from his job as a loan processor when the real estate market began to decline. Then, after finding work as a project manager for a plumbing company, he was hit by layoffs again.

“It’s kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want,” he said.

Clardy said his goal is to contact at least 10 potential employers each day by phone, letter and the Internet. Being unemployed, he has found, is hard work, too.

“It was a scramble,” Clardy said. “I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs.”

The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday’s event, which they said drew about 10,000 people. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair to fill some 500 part-time jobs at the stadium during baseball season attracted about 7,000 applicants.

California’s unemployment rate stands at 10.1 percent, a full 2 percentage points higher than the national rate. The state’s Employment Development Department estimates that nearly half a million California residents have lost their jobs in the past year.

“We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago,” said Gloria Bratton Moore, who runs the state-funded Work Source job center in Los Angeles. Nonetheless, she added, “There are jobs available.”

At Dodger Stadium, however, it was clear that competition for those available positions was intense. Applicants often stood four and five deep in front of employer tables, leaving most of the 10,000 job seekers with little chance to make a lasting impression.

Still, organizers worked hard to lift spirits.

“Yes we can. Yes we can,” Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia chanted over a loudspeaker.

State lawmaker Kevin deLeon told the crowd that they were among the nation’s hardest hit by the economic downturn, but urged them not to give up.

“We will get out of this economic funk,” he said. “We will recover soon. We’ve got to have hope.”

Garcia’s and deLeon’s remarks echoed the campaign slogans of President Obama, who recently won approval of a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package.

Recruiters from government agencies at the job fair said that funding would begin creating jobs within the next few months. The Army Corps of Engineers told applicants it was hiring for a wide range of positions, including engineers, heavy-equipment operators and environmental field workers. The Commerce Department is adding more than 1 million jobs in preparation for the 2010 census, and other federal agencies are hiring as well.

All of this was encouraging news for Clardy, who left resumes and completed applications at several of the 80 booths spread across the stadium parking lot. Still, he remained realistic about whether the day’s efforts would lead directly to employment.

“It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview,” he said. “Now it doesn’t seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore.”

**Thousands line up for jobs at Dodger Stadium as recession squeezes Los Angeles workers**

**LOS ANGELES** — Long before the gates opened at Dodger Stadium, the line of job seekers wrapped across the parking lot, a crowd more often seen on summer game days than at a weekday employment fair.

But there were no jerseys, no hot dogs and no cheers from the stands. Instead, thousands of people carried résumés, dressed in pressed shirts and business shoes, hoping to land work in one of the toughest job markets in years.

Among them was **Eric Clardy**, an unemployed Los Angeles resident who said he had been out of steady work for months.

“I never thought I’d be standing in a line this long just to get a chance to talk to somebody,” Clardy said, holding a folder of résumés. “But right now, you do what you have to do. I need a job. My family needs me to get a job.”

The massive hiring event, held inside and around Dodger Stadium, drew job seekers from across Southern California as the recession continued to batter workers and businesses. Organizers said **tens of thousands of people were expected to attend**, with applicants competing for positions ranging from retail and warehouse work to health care, customer service, security, hospitality and transportation.

More than **100 employers and agencies** were represented, including companies looking to fill immediate openings in grocery stores, hospitals, call centers, delivery operations, restaurants, hotels and government services. Some employers said they were hiring seasonal workers, while others were seeking full-time employees with benefits.

“We have jobs available today,” said one recruiter for a logistics company hiring drivers and warehouse staff. “But we also have a lot more applicants than openings. People need to be prepared, professional and patient.”

California had been among the states hit hardest by the recession, with unemployment hovering in double digits in many communities. In Los Angeles County, job losses in construction, manufacturing, entertainment support services and retail had left many workers searching for months.

For Clardy, the stadium job fair represented both frustration and hope.

“I’ve applied online. I’ve gone door to door. Sometimes you don’t hear anything back,” he said. “At least here, I can look somebody in the eye and tell them I’m ready to work.”

Inside the stadium concourse, job seekers moved from table to table, shaking hands with recruiters and filling out applications. Some stood in lines 50 people deep to speak with companies offering health care or municipal jobs. Others took advantage of résumé workshops and interview coaching offered on-site.

Employers said they were looking for applicants with flexibility — workers willing to take night shifts, temporary assignments or lower pay than they once earned.

“That’s the reality right now,” said a human resources manager at the fair. “People who may have had one career for 15 or 20 years are now considering something completely different.”

For many in attendance, the recession had erased any stigma about asking for help. Former managers stood beside recent graduates. Parents brought children with them. Some applicants said they had burned through savings; others said unemployment benefits were close to running out.

Clardy said he was open to almost anything.

“I’m not coming in here saying I have to have the perfect job,” he said. “I’m saying give me a chance. Let me prove myself.”

City officials and event organizers said the turnout underscored the scale of the economic pain across the region. While the number of employers hiring offered some encouragement, they acknowledged that the demand for work far exceeded the available jobs.

Still, for job seekers like Clardy, the day offered something that had been in short supply: a possibility.

“You see all these people and you realize you’re not alone,” he said. “But I’m trying to stay positive. Somebody here is hiring. I just need one yes.”

**Los Angeles** — With the Dodgers away in Arizona for spring training, the parking lots outside Dodger Stadium took on a different purpose this week: helping Angelenos get back to work.

Hundreds of job seekers gathered outside the ballpark for a large-scale employment fair hosted by the City of Los Angeles, county workforce agencies and community partners. Instead of tailgates and game-day traffic, the stadium grounds were filled with employer booths, résumé tables and long lines of applicants hoping to land interviews.

Companies including **Coca-Cola**, **Lowe’s**, local logistics firms, health care providers, hospitality businesses and city contractors were on hand to recruit workers for full-time, part-time and seasonal positions. Many employers said they were looking to fill jobs quickly, with some conducting preliminary interviews on site.

Public officials called the event a practical use of one of the city’s most recognizable venues during the baseball offseason.

“Dodger Stadium is a place where Los Angeles comes together,” one city official said. “Today, it’s not about baseball — it’s about opportunity, paychecks and connecting people to work.”

Representatives from the mayor’s office, the Los Angeles City Council and county workforce development programs attended the fair, encouraging residents to take advantage of job training, résumé assistance and public employment services. Organizers said the goal was not only to connect applicants with immediate openings but also to provide pathways into long-term careers.

For many attendees, the job fair came at a critical time.

**Marcus Hill**, 42, of South Los Angeles, said he has been unemployed for nearly six months after losing his warehouse job last year. Dressed in a button-down shirt and carrying a folder of résumés, Hill said he arrived early hoping to speak directly with hiring managers.

“Applying online feels like sending your résumé into a black hole,” Hill said. “Here, I can shake somebody’s hand. I can tell them I’m ready to work.”

Hill said he was especially interested in openings with Lowe’s and Coca-Cola, both of which had recruiters speaking with applicants about warehouse, delivery, merchandising and customer service roles.

“I’m not looking for anything fancy,” he said. “I’m looking for steady hours, benefits and a chance to get back on my feet.”

Employers said in-person events remain valuable, particularly for applicants who may struggle with online hiring systems or who want to make a direct impression.

Workforce counselors met with attendees to discuss skills certification programs in fields such as construction, health care, transportation and information technology.

“Employment is one of the most important tools we have for strengthening communities,” a county workforce representative said. “When people can access good jobs, families become more stable and neighborhoods become stronger.”

As job seekers moved from booth to booth beneath the stadium’s towering lights, the setting served as a reminder of the city’s shifting rhythms. The Dodgers may be preparing for a new season elsewhere, but in their absence, the stadium became a hub for another kind of hope.

For Hill, the day ended with two follow-up interviews and a sense of optimism he said he had not felt in months.

“That’s all I needed,” he said. “Just a door to open.”

**At Dodger Stadium, a Different Kind of Line Forms: Thousands Seek Work in a Hard Economy**

LOS ANGELES — On game days, the crowds at Dodger Stadium come looking for hot dogs, fly balls and a few hours of escape. But on this gray weekday morning, the people streaming through the gates carried résumés instead of scorecards.

Among them was **Eric Clardy**, a laid-off loan processor from California, dressed carefully for the occasion: pressed shirt, polished shoes, a folder of résumés tucked under one arm. He had come not to cheer, but to compete — one applicant among thousands at a job fair that turned the stadium concourse into a snapshot of the recession.

Clardy used to help process home loans, part of an industry that once seemed to move as fast as California’s housing market. Then the market collapsed, offices shrank, and the work disappeared. Like many who arrived at the stadium, he had spent months answering online postings, refreshing job boards and waiting for phone calls that rarely came.

“I’m just trying to get back to work,” he said, standing in a line that curved past concession stands and concrete pillars. “At this point, you do what you have to do.”

The job fair drew thousands of people from across Southern California — former clerks, sales workers, mortgage employees, recent graduates, middle-aged professionals and parents trying to hold their households together. Some wore suits. Others came in work boots. Many held folders thick with résumés, evidence of an economy in which one opening could attract hundreds of hopefuls.

Employers sat behind folding tables beneath stadium signs usually meant to guide fans to their seats. The available jobs ranged from retail and security to customer service and administrative work. For applicants like Clardy, even positions outside their field were worth pursuing.

“I’ve got experience. I know how to deal with paperwork, customers, deadlines,” he said. “But there are a lot of people here who can say the same thing.”

That was the hard truth visible everywhere: the recession had not only taken jobs, it had crowded the path back to employment. People who once expected to move steadily through careers now found themselves waiting in long lines for a brief conversation with a recruiter.

Some applicants compared notes about unemployment benefits and overdue bills. Others quietly rehearsed their introductions. A few had brought children, unable to arrange child care. The mood was patient but tense — hopeful enough to wait, anxious enough to know that waiting might not be enough.

Clardy moved from table to table, shaking hands, asking questions and leaving behind résumés. Each exchange lasted only minutes. Then he would step aside, make a note, and join the next line.

For him, the search had become a job of its own. Mornings began with applications. Afternoons were spent following leads. Evenings brought calculations: rent, gas, groceries, how long savings could stretch. He said he was willing to take less pay than before, willing to commute, willing to start over if that was what the market demanded.

Around him, the stadium’s familiar vastness made the moment feel even larger. The empty seats rose in blue rows above the concourse, a reminder of crowds that usually gather for entertainment. Down below, the crowd had come for something more urgent.

By midday, the lines had not shortened. Recruiters continued collecting résumés in stacks. Applicants kept arriving, some after long drives from inland communities hit hard by foreclosures and layoffs.

Clardy knew there would be no guarantee of a call, no promise that handing over a résumé at Dodger Stadium would change anything. Still, he stayed.

“You have to keep showing up,” he said.

In a recession measured by unemployment rates and market losses, the job fair offered a more personal accounting: thousands of people standing shoulder to shoulder, trying to reclaim a paycheck, a routine, a sense of control. For Eric Clardy, and for many around him, the day was not about finding the perfect job. It was about finding a way forward.

**California Job Seekers Crowd Dodger Stadium as Unemployment Rises**

*Los Angeles* — Thousands of job seekers streamed into Dodger Stadium for a large employment event this week, underscoring the severity of California’s labor market downturn as the state continues to grapple with rising unemployment and a shortage of available jobs.

The event drew applicants from across Southern California, many of them recently laid off from construction, retail, hospitality, manufacturing, and office-support positions. Long lines formed outside the stadium as attendees waited to meet employers, submit résumés, and search for any sign of steady work in an increasingly competitive job market.

California’s unemployment rate has climbed sharply amid the broader national recession, leaving many workers facing months without a paycheck. The slowdown has hit the state especially hard, with the housing collapse, credit crisis, and reduced consumer spending forcing businesses to cut payrolls or freeze hiring. For many families, unemployment benefits, savings, and part-time work have become temporary lifelines.

At the Dodger Stadium hiring event, job seekers moved from booth to booth looking for openings in fields ranging from security and customer service to health care, transportation, government work, and entry-level office jobs. But the number of applicants appeared to far exceed the positions available, creating intense competition even for modest-paying jobs.

Some attendees said they had applied to dozens of employers online without receiving a response. Others said they were willing to accept lower wages, longer commutes, or work outside their previous careers if it meant getting back on a payroll.

The pressure has increased expectations for government action. President Barack Obama’s economic stimulus package, approved in response to the recession, was designed in part to stabilize state budgets, fund infrastructure projects, support unemployment benefits, and create or preserve jobs. California officials have looked to stimulus money to help blunt the downturn, though many job seekers say relief has been slow to reach them directly.

One notable source of temporary employment has been federal hiring connected to the U.S. Census. Census jobs have offered short-term opportunities for thousands of workers nationwide, including in California, where canvassing, clerical, and field positions have attracted strong interest. While those jobs provide income for some, economists caution that temporary census hiring is not enough to offset the broader losses in the private sector.

Employers at the stadium said they were looking for applicants with flexibility, reliability, and strong customer-service skills. Several also noted that the large turnout reflected a labor market in which companies can choose from a deep pool of qualified candidates, including workers with years of experience now applying for entry-level positions.

Workforce officials said events like the one at Dodger Stadium can help connect applicants with employers more efficiently, but they also acknowledged the scale of the challenge. With job openings limited and layoffs continuing in some industries, many workers remain trapped in a cycle of applications, interviews, and rejection.

Economists say California’s recovery will likely depend on a combination of federal support, renewed consumer spending, business confidence, and growth in sectors such as health care, clean energy, logistics, and technology. Until then, scenes like the one at Dodger Stadium may remain common: thousands of workers competing for a relatively small number of openings, hoping that the next handshake or submitted résumé leads to a job.
